claim: The divergence between vertebrate and invertebrate lineages occurred over 600 million years ago.
source: It is estimated that the divergence between vertebrate and invertebrate lineages occurred over 600 million years ago (Hedges et al., 2006; Peterson et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hedges et al., 2006 and Peterson et al., 2008

claim: After the divergence between vertebrates and invertebrates, protein coding sequences have retained a relatively high level of similarity.
source: After the divergence, protein coding sequences have retained a relatively high level of similarity, whereas homology in gene-regulatory elements is not detectable, despite the fact that many developmental pathways and regulatory relationships between TFs and their target genes have been conserved (see e g., Goodrich et al., 1996; Pichaud and Desplan, 2002; Ciglar and Furlong, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodrich et al., 1996; Pichaud and Desplan, 2002; Ciglar and Furlong, 2009

claim: Homology in gene-regulatory elements is not detectable between vertebrates and invertebrates despite conserved developmental pathways.
source: After the divergence, protein coding sequences have retained a relatively high level of similarity, whereas homology in gene-regulatory elements is not detectable, despite the fact that many developmental pathways and regulatory relationships between TFs and their target genes have been conserved (see e g., Goodrich et al., 1996; Pichaud and Desplan, 2002; Ciglar and Furlong, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodrich et al., 1996; Pichaud and Desplan, 2002; Ciglar and Furlong, 2009

claim: Many developmental pathways and regulatory relationships between TFs and their target genes have been conserved between vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: After the divergence, protein coding sequences have retained a relatively high level of similarity, whereas homology in gene-regulatory elements is not detectable, despite the fact that many developmental pathways and regulatory relationships between TFs and their target genes have been conserved (see e g., Goodrich et al., 1996; Pichaud and Desplan, 2002; Ciglar and Furlong, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goodrich et al., 1996; Pichaud and Desplan, 2002; Ciglar and Furlong, 2009

claim: Some changes in coding sequences of TFs have been observed and linked to specific evolutionary adaptations.
source: Some changes in coding sequences of TFs have indeed been observed, and linked to specific evolutionary adaptations (Enard et al., 2002; Di-Poï et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Enard et al., 2002 and Di-Poï et al., 2010

claim: Primary TF DNA binding specificity evolves slowly and is extremely conserved between mammalian species.
source: Several studies have indicated that primary TF DNA binding specificity evolves slowly, and is extremely conserved between mammalian species (see e g., Bohmann et al., 1987; Struhl, 1987; Merika and Orkin, 1993; Amoutzias et al., 2007; Wei et al., 2010; Jolma et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations including Bohmann et al., 1987; Struhl, 1987; Merika and Orkin, 1993; Amoutzias et al., 2007; Wei et al., 2010; Jolma et al., 2013

claim: The origin of most structural families of TFs dates well before the emergence of mammals.
source: The origin of most structural families of TFs dates well before the emergence of mammals, and even predates the divergence of vertebrates and invertebrates.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about TF evolution

claim: The origin of most structural families of TFs predates the divergence of vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: The origin of most structural families of TFs dates well before the emergence of mammals, and even predates the divergence of vertebrates and invertebrates.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about TF evolution

claim: Within each TF family, DNA binding specificity has diverged considerably, with many families having 2–10 different subclasses displaying different primary binding specificities.
source: Within each TF family, DNA binding specificity has also diverged considerably, with many families having 2–10 different subclasses displaying different primary binding specificities (Berger et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2010; Jolma et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berger et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2010; Jolma et al., 2013

claim: Many differences in the TF repertoire between invertebrates and vertebrates exist due to the expansion of some gene families, such as nuclear receptors and C2H2 zinc finger factors in vertebrates.
source: In addition, many differences in the TF repertoire between invertebrates and vertebrates exist due to the expansion of some gene families, such as nuclear receptors and C2H2 zinc finger factors in vertebrates (Charoensawan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Charoensawan et al., 2010

claim: The binding specificities of 242 Drosophila TFs were determined in this study.
source: To address this, we determined the binding specificities of 242 Drosophila TFs, and compared them to human and mouse data.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented

claim: TF binding specificities are highly conserved between Drosophila and mammals.
source: This analysis revealed that TF binding specificities are highly conserved between Drosophila and mammals, and that for orthologous TFs, the similarity extends even to the level of very subtle dinucleotide binding preferences.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the comparative analysis of HT-SELEX data

claim: For orthologous TFs, the similarity in binding specificity extends to the level of very subtle dinucleotide binding preferences.
source: This analysis revealed that TF binding specificities are highly conserved between Drosophila and mammals, and that for orthologous TFs, the similarity extends even to the level of very subtle dinucleotide binding preferences.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the comparative analysis of HT-SELEX data

claim: The few human TFs with divergent specificities function in cell types not found in fruit flies.
source: The few human TFs with divergent specificities function in cell types not found in fruit flies, suggesting that evolution of TF specificities contributes to emergence of novel types of differentiated cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the analysis of TF functions

claim: Evolution of TF specificities contributes to emergence of novel types of differentiated cells.
source: The few human TFs with divergent specificities function in cell types not found in fruit flies, suggesting that evolution of TF specificities contributes to emergence of novel types of differentiated cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that divergent TFs function in cell types not found in fruit flies

claim: A collection of 760 DNA-binding domains and 633 full-length Drosophila TF constructs were compiled for this study.
source: A collection of cDNAs of DNA binding domains (DBDs) and full-length Drosophila TFs were compiled based on annotations in FlyTF.org (Pfreundt et al., 2010) and Hens et al. (2011), respectively. A total of 760 DBDs and 633 full length fruit fly TF constructs were expressed in E. coli as N-terminal thioredoxin-HIS tag fusion proteins, and subjected to the HT-SELEX process (Figure 1; Supplementary file 1A–C; see 'Materials and methods' for details).
evidence: This is a methodological detail supported by the experimental data

claim: The clone collections covered 271/294 (92%) of 'trusted TFs' and 612/754 (81%) of 'putative TFs' in FlyTF.org.
source: Together, the clone collections covered 271/294 (92%) and 612/754 (81%) of 'trusted TFs' and 'putative TFs' in FlyTF.org (Pfreundt et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the coverage of the study, supported by the experimental data

claim: Robustly enriched subsequences were identified for a total of 196 DBDs and 92 full-length TF proteins, representing 242 unique fruit fly TFs.
source: The obtained sequences were analyzed computationally, resulting in the identification of robustly enriched subsequences for a total of 196 DBDs and 92 full-length TF proteins, representing a total of 242 unique fruit fly TFs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the computational analysis of HT-SELEX data

claim: Motifs were obtained for 86% of fruit fly TF families.
source: Motifs were obtained for 86% of fruit fly TF families, with median within-family coverage of 49% (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study, supported by Figure 1B

claim: The median within-family coverage of motifs was 49%.
source: Motifs were obtained for 86% of fruit fly TF families, with median within-family coverage of 49% (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study, supported by Figure 1B

claim: A relatively low success rate was observed for C2H2 zinc fingers and basic helix-loop-helix proteins.
source: Similar to earlier studies (Badis et al., 2009; Jolma et al., 2013), a relatively low success rate was observed for C2H2 zinc fingers and basic helix-loop-helix proteins, probably at least in part due to difficulty in computational identification of DNA-binding zinc finger proteins, and the fact that many bHLH proteins bind to DNA as obligate heterodimers.
evidence: This observation is supported by the experimental data and comparison with earlier studies

claim: The low success rate for C2H2 zinc fingers is probably at least in part due to difficulty in computational identification of DNA-binding zinc finger proteins.
source: Similar to earlier studies (Badis et al., 2009; Jolma et al., 2013), a relatively low success rate was observed for C2H2 zinc fingers and basic helix-loop-helix proteins, probably at least in part due to difficulty in computational identification of DNA-binding zinc finger proteins, and the fact that many bHLH proteins bind to DNA as obligate heterodimers.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed low success rate

claim: Many bHLH proteins bind to DNA as obligate heterodimers.
source: Similar to earlier studies (Badis et al., 2009; Jolma et al., 2013), a relatively low success rate was observed for C2H2 zinc fingers and basic helix-loop-helix proteins, probably at least in part due to difficulty in computational identification of DNA-binding zinc finger proteins, and the fact that many bHLH proteins bind to DNA as obligate heterodimers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bHLH proteins

claim: A relatively low success rate was observed for large DBD constructs and full-length proteins, probably due to difficulty of expressing them in an active form in E. coli.
source: In addition, relatively low success rate was observed for large DBD constructs and full-length proteins, probably due to difficulty of expressing them in an active form in E. coli.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data with a speculative explanation

claim: A novel algorithm called Autoseed was developed to identify enriched subsequences in HT-SELEX experiments.
source: To improve the detection of enriched subsequences in the HT-SELEX experiments, we developed a novel algorithm, Autoseed, that identifies all subsequences that represent local maxima, that is, are enriched more than any closely related sequence.
evidence: This is a methodological development described in the study

claim: Autoseed identifies all subsequences that represent local maxima, that is, are enriched more than any closely related sequence.
source: To improve the detection of enriched subsequences in the HT-SELEX experiments, we developed a novel algorithm, Autoseed, that identifies all subsequences that represent local maxima, that is, are enriched more than any closely related sequence.
evidence: This is a description of the Autoseed algorithm

claim: The Autoseed method is based on a novel distance measure between two subsequences called the Huddinge distance.
source: The method is based on a novel distance measure between two subsequences, the Huddinge distance (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and 'Material and methods' for details).
evidence: This is a methodological detail described in the study and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The Autoseed method can identify diverse motifs with widely spaced recognition sites.
source: The method compares also gapped subsequences to ungapped ones, and can thus identify diverse motifs with widely spaced recognition sites, and differentiate between monomers and dimers of the same subsequence.
evidence: This is a description of the capabilities of the Autoseed method

claim: The Autoseed method can differentiate between monomers and dimers of the same subsequence.
source: The method compares also gapped subsequences to ungapped ones, and can thus identify diverse motifs with widely spaced recognition sites, and differentiate between monomers and dimers of the same subsequence.
evidence: This is a description of the capabilities of the Autoseed method

claim: The Autoseed method can identify strong dinucleotide preferences.
source: In addition, as subsequences that differ by more than one substitution are not compared to each other, the method can identify strong dinucleotide preferences.
evidence: This is a description of the capabilities of the Autoseed method

claim: Analysis of the fruit fly HT-SELEX dataset using Autoseed resulted in the identification of 416 motifs.
source: Analysis of the fruit fly HT-SELEX dataset using Autoseed resulted in the identification of 416 motifs, of which 210 were monomeric, 198 dimeric, 5 trimeric, and 3 dimers of dimers (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the Autoseed analysis, supported by Figure 1C

claim: Of the 416 motifs identified, 210 were monomeric, 198 dimeric, 5 trimeric, and 3 dimers of dimers.
source: Analysis of the fruit fly HT-SELEX dataset using Autoseed resulted in the identification of 416 motifs, of which 210 were monomeric, 198 dimeric, 5 trimeric, and 3 dimers of dimers (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative breakdown of the motif types, supported by Figure 1C

claim: 90 of the 416 motifs describe secondary binding modes.
source: Of these motifs, 90 describe secondary binding modes—bound sequences that are distinctly different from the primary TF binding site (see Badis et al., 2009; Rohs et al., 2010; Jolma et al., 2013) for a TF that has a stronger primary binding motif.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis, with reference to previous work defining secondary binding modes

claim: Of the secondary models, 29 cases were due to strong dinucleotide preferences, 21 cases were due to flanking sequence variants, and 40 cases were due to spacing and orientation preferences.
source: Of the secondary models, 29 cases were due to strong dinucleotide preferences, 21 cases were due to flanking sequence variants, and 40 cases were due to spacing and orientation preferences (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative breakdown of the types of secondary models, supported by Figure 1D

claim: Different TF structural families have clearly divergent specificities.
source: As suggested by previous studies (Wei et al., 2010; Jolma et al., 2013; Weirauch et al., 2014), different TF structural families had clearly divergent specificities, and amino-acid sequence similarity was predictive of overall DNA binding specificity in most TF families.
evidence: This observation is supported by the data and consistent with previous studies

claim: Amino-acid sequence similarity is predictive of overall DNA binding specificity in most TF families.
source: As suggested by previous studies (Wei et al., 2010; Jolma et al., 2013; Weirauch et al., 2014), different TF structural families had clearly divergent specificities, and amino-acid sequence similarity was predictive of overall DNA binding specificity in most TF families.
evidence: This observation is supported by the data and consistent with previous studies

claim: Fruit fly bHLH proteins can be classified into six subfamilies based on their preferred 6 bp core motifs.
source: For example, we could classify fruit fly bHLH proteins into six subfamilies based on their preferred 6 bp core motifs (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of bHLH proteins, supported by Figure 2

claim: Members of bHLH proteins that are similar in amino-acid sequence generally recognize the same core sequence.
source: Members that are similar in amino-acid sequence generally recognized the same core sequence, and highly similar TFs recognized also similar flanking nucleotides (e.g., HLHm3, HLHmbeta, HLHmgamma, HLHmdelta).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of bHLH proteins

claim: Highly similar bHLH TFs recognize similar flanking nucleotides.
source: Members that are similar in amino-acid sequence generally recognized the same core sequence, and highly similar TFs recognized also similar flanking nucleotides (e.g., HLHm3, HLHmbeta, HLHmgamma, HLHmdelta).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of bHLH proteins, with specific examples provided

claim: Order based on similarity of TF DNA binding specificities largely recapitulates the phylogenetic relationships between the DBDs.
source: Order based on similarity of TF DNA binding specificities, calculated using correlations between scores of all possible gapped 6 bp subsequences (see 'Materials and methods' for details), largely recapitulated the phylogenetic relationships between the DBDs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative analysis, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The profiles obtained for proteins analyzed using B1H showed, with very few exceptions, the same core binding specificities as those obtained by HT-SELEX.
source: The profiles we obtained for the proteins that had been analyzed using B1H showed, with very few exceptions, the same core binding specificities (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparison between HT-SELEX and B1H data, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Motifs obtained using HT-SELEX and B1H for the same proteins were often not located next to each other in the dendrogram.
source: Motifs generally clustered based on the corresponding TF families. However, motifs obtained using HT-SELEX and B1H for the same proteins were often not located next to each other.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparative analysis of HT-SELEX and B1H data

claim: Flanking sequences obtained using HT-SELEX and B1H are often not identical.
source: One reason for this is that flanking sequences obtained using HT-SELEX and B1H are often not identical.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparative analysis of HT-SELEX and B1H data

claim: HT-SELEX data generally yield longer profiles than B1H data (average width of 12.7 bp vs 10.7 bp).
source: The HT-SELEX data also generally yield somewhat longer profiles (average width of 12.7 bp vs 10.7 bp), particularly in cases where TFs bind as dimers (e.g., nuclear receptors).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between HT-SELEX and B1H data

claim: Inclusion of dimeric sites and extended flanking specificity improve prediction of in vivo occupied sites.
source: We and others have shown earlier that inclusion of dimeric sites and the extended flanking specificity improve prediction of in vivo occupied sites (Jolma et al., 2013; Orenstein and Shamir, 2014), indicating that the extended specificity information revealed by HT-SELEX is biologically relevant.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jolma et al., 2013 and Orenstein and Shamir, 2014

claim: The extended specificity information revealed by HT-SELEX is biologically relevant.
source: We and others have shown earlier that inclusion of dimeric sites and the extended flanking specificity improve prediction of in vivo occupied sites (Jolma et al., 2013; Orenstein and Shamir, 2014), indicating that the extended specificity information revealed by HT-SELEX is biologically relevant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the improved prediction of in vivo occupied sites

claim: The HT-SELEX data include binding models for 65 genes which are not included in the B1H collection.
source: In addition, the HT-SELEX data include binding models for 65 genes, which are not included in the B1H collection (Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between the HT-SELEX and B1H datasets

claim: The HT-SELEX dataset and the existing B1H dataset support each other but have method-specific differences and do not overlap completely.
source: In conclusion, our dataset and the existing B1H dataset support each other, but appear to have method-specific differences and do not overlap completely.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the comparison of HT-SELEX and B1H data

claim: Sequence analysis of DBD sequences of Drosophila and human revealed substantial differences in conservation of orthologous TF DBD pairs both between and within different TF families.
source: However, sequence analysis of DBD sequences of Drosophila and human revealed substantial differences in conservation of orthologous TF DBD pairs both between and within different TF families (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that some divergence of TF binding specificity could have occurred.
evidence: This is a result from the sequence analysis, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Comparison of HT-SELEX derived fruit fly and mammalian TF profiles indicates that fruit fly and human homeodomains bind to a similar range of sequences.
source: However, this result could be due to the method-specific differences discussed above rather than true evolutionary divergence. Indeed, comparison between our HT-SELEX derived fruit fly and mammalian TF profiles indicate that fruit fly and human homeodomains bind to a similar range of sequences (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative analysis of HT-SELEX data, supported by Figure 3B

claim: Comparison of HT-SELEX results for orthologous proteins from human and fruit fly yields very similar specificity profiles.
source: In contrast, comparison of our results generated using the same method yields very similar specificity profiles between orthologous proteins from human and fruit fly (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative analysis of HT-SELEX data, supported by Figure 3C–E

claim: Analysis of in vivo motifs for Nkx and EGR proteins supports the motif derived by HT-SELEX.
source: Consistently with this finding, analysis of in vivo motifs for Nkx and EGR proteins supports the motif derived by HT-SELEX (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a validation of HT-SELEX results using in vivo data, supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Fruit fly DNA-binding specificities cover almost the complete range of mammalian TF specificities.
source: A global comparison between fruit fly and mammalian TF binding specificities also revealed that fruit fly DNA-binding specificities cover almost the complete range of mammalian TF specificities (Figure 4), and that clustering of motifs is not influenced by the species indicating that orthologous proteins recognize highly conserved motifs.
evidence: This is a result from the global comparison of TF binding specificities, supported by Figure 4

claim: Clustering of motifs is not influenced by the species, indicating that orthologous proteins recognize highly conserved motifs.
source: A global comparison between fruit fly and mammalian TF binding specificities also revealed that fruit fly DNA-binding specificities cover almost the complete range of mammalian TF specificities (Figure 4), and that clustering of motifs is not influenced by the species indicating that orthologous proteins recognize highly conserved motifs.
evidence: This is a result from the global comparison of TF binding specificities, supported by Figure 4

claim: The gene regulatory code that determines how DNA sequence directs gene expression is highly conserved in evolution.
source: These results indicate that the gene regulatory code that determines how DNA sequence directs gene expression is highly conserved in evolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the conservation of TF binding specificities

claim: In all cases where sufficiently high quality data existed for detection of weaker binding sites in both species, the secondary modes of binding were conserved.
source: In all cases where sufficiently high quality data existed for detection of weaker binding sites in both species, the secondary modes were conserved (Figure 5A and not shown), indicating that TF specificity does not commonly evolve by loss or gain of secondary binding modes.
evidence: This is a result from the comparative analysis of secondary binding modes, supported by Figure 5A

claim: TF specificity does not commonly evolve by loss or gain of secondary binding modes.
source: In all cases where sufficiently high quality data existed for detection of weaker binding sites in both species, the secondary modes were conserved (Figure 5A and not shown), indicating that TF specificity does not commonly evolve by loss or gain of secondary binding modes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the conservation of secondary binding modes

claim: Dinucleotide preferences of TFs are conserved between fruit flies and humans.
source: Analysis of conservation of such dinucleotide preferences in several TF families, including homeobox, heat shock factor, and nuclear receptors indicated that in all cases, even the dinucleotide preferences of the TFs were conserved between fruit flies and humans (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of dinucleotide preferences, supported by Figure 5C–E

claim: Orthologous TFs bind to DNA in a very similar manner, resulting in conservation of even the secondary DNA binding modes and subtle dinucleotide preferences.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that orthologous TFs bind to DNA in a very similar manner, resulting in conservation of even the secondary DNA binding modes and subtle dinucleotide preferences.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analysis of secondary binding modes and dinucleotide preferences

claim: Brinker is a TF class that recognizes a unique site and exists in fruit flies but not in humans.
source: However, both fruit flies and humans have a TF class that recognizes a unique site and does not exist in the other lineage, brinker and interferon regulatory factor (IRF) TFs, respectively.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparative analysis of TF specificities

claim: Interferon regulatory factor (IRF) TFs are a TF class that recognizes a unique site and exists in humans but not in fruit flies.
source: However, both fruit flies and humans have a TF class that recognizes a unique site and does not exist in the other lineage, brinker and interferon regulatory factor (IRF) TFs, respectively.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparative analysis of TF specificities

claim: Fruit fly lacks monomeric TFs that recognize sites similar to those of non-canonical E2F repressors (E2F7 and E2F8).
source: For example, our analysis indicates that fruit fly lacks monomeric TFs that recognize sites similar to those of non-canonical E2F repressors (E2F7 and E2F8; see Jolma et al., 2013) and members of the class III ETS family (Wei et al., 2010) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and data not shown).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative analysis, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and citations

claim: Fruit fly lacks monomeric TFs that recognize sites similar to those of members of the class III ETS family.
source: For example, our analysis indicates that fruit fly lacks monomeric TFs that recognize sites similar to those of non-canonical E2F repressors (E2F7 and E2F8; see Jolma et al., 2013) and members of the class III ETS family (Wei et al., 2010) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and data not shown).
evidence: This is a result from the comparative analysis, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and citations

claim: Drosophila has only one protein (ERR) that is homologous to human nuclear receptor group that includes AR, ESR, and ESRR subgroups.
source: In addition, Drosophila has only one protein (ERR) that is homologous to human nuclear receptor group that includes three subgroups, androgen receptor (AR), estrogen receptor (ESR), and estrogen-receptor related protein (ESRR) subgroups.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparative analysis of nuclear receptors

claim: The fruit fly ERR protein recognizes a site that is similar to that recognized by human ESRR.
source: The fruit fly ERR protein recognizes a site that is similar to that recognized by human ESRR.
evidence: This is a result from the comparative analysis of binding specificities

claim: No fruit fly orthologs exist for any of the proteins in the ESR or AR subgroups.
source: However, no fruit fly orthologs exist for any of the proteins in the ESR or AR subgroups, which recognize different sites (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation from the comparative analysis, supported by Figure 6A

claim: The fruit fly knirps-like (knrl) nuclear receptor (NR0 subfamily) has no orthologs in human.
source: Conversely, the fruit fly knirps-like (knrl) nuclear receptor (NR0 subfamily) has no orthologs in human (King-Jones and Thummel, 2005) and its motif is distinct from the other NR proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is supported by citation to King-Jones and Thummel, 2005 and Figure 1—figure supplement 9

claim: The motif of knirps-like (knrl) is distinct from the other NR proteins.
source: Conversely, the fruit fly knirps-like (knrl) nuclear receptor (NR0 subfamily) has no orthologs in human (King-Jones and Thummel, 2005) and its motif is distinct from the other NR proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of binding specificities, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 9

claim: The Pax family transcription factor, Poxn, has no ortholog in human.
source: Similarly, the Pax family transcription factor, Poxn, has no ortholog in human (Hill et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hill et al., 2010

claim: While other Pax TFs recognize a monomeric Paired binding site, Poxn binds to a dimeric variant of the site.
source: While other Pax TFs recognize a monomeric Paired binding site, Poxn binds to a dimeric variant of the site (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of Pax TF binding specificities, supported by Figure 6B

claim: TF DNA-binding specificity can evolve via duplication and divergence.
source: These results indicate that TF DNA-binding specificity can evolve via duplication and divergence, and that such changes can yield novel DNA-binding specificities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations of species-specific TF specificities

claim: Duplication and divergence of TFs can yield novel DNA-binding specificities.
source: These results indicate that TF DNA-binding specificity can evolve via duplication and divergence, and that such changes can yield novel DNA-binding specificities.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations of species-specific TF specificities

claim: CG30420 (also known as Atf-2) is an ortholog of mammalian ATF2 and ATF7.
source: CG30420 (also known as Atf-2) is an ortholog of mammalian ATF2 and ATF7 (Sano et al., 2005; Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sano et al., 2005 and Figure 7A

claim: CG30420 recognizes a GACGT(C/G) sequence, whereas all other Atf subfamily genes including ATF7 and ATF2 recognize GACGT(C/A).
source: This gene recognizes a GACGT(C/G) sequence, whereas all other Atf subfamily genes including ATF7 and ATF2 recognize GACGT(C/A) (Figure 7B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of binding specificities, supported by Figure 7B and Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: CG30420 can recognize a larger variety of sequences than ATF2 or ATF7.
source: Analysis of enrichment of 10 bp subsequences (10-mers) indicates that one set of 10-mers containing GACGT(C/A) are enriched by both CG30420 and ATF7, whereas 10-mers containing GACGTG sequences are enriched only by CG30420 (Figure 7C), indicating that CG30420 can recognize a larger variety of sequences than ATF2 or ATF7.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of 10-mer enrichment, supported by Figure 7C

claim: The specificity of CG30420 was observed for both DBD and full-length TF, and was reproducible using a completely independent DBD expression construct.
source: The specificity of CG30420 was observed for both DBD and full-length TF, and also reproducible using a completely independent DBD expression construct.
evidence: This is a validation of the CG30420 specificity result

claim: A key asparagine that hydrogen bonds to the cytosine base in other CRE/ATF bZIP proteins is replaced by an arginine in CG30420.
source: Consistently with the change in specificity, a key asparagine that hydrogen bonds to the cytosine base in other CRE/ATF bZIP proteins is replaced by an arginine in CG30420 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a structural observation that explains the change in specificity, supported by Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: All human NR1I subfamily genes (VDR, NR1I2, NR1I3) recognize a motif containing direct repeat of a GTTCA motif.
source: Similarly, Hr96, a Drosophila NR1J group nuclear receptor gene recognizes tail-to-tail repetitive GT(A/G)CA motifs while the related human NR1 genes recognize head-to-tail repetitive GTTCA motifs (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of nuclear receptor binding specificities, supported by Figure 7D,E

claim: Hr96, a Drosophila NR1J group nuclear receptor gene, recognizes tail-to-tail repetitive GT(A/G)CA motifs.
source: Similarly, Hr96, a Drosophila NR1J group nuclear receptor gene recognizes tail-to-tail repetitive GT(A/G)CA motifs while the related human NR1 genes recognize head-to-tail repetitive GTTCA motifs (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of nuclear receptor binding specificities, supported by Figure 7D,E

claim: The class IV ETS family protein SPDEF and its ortholog Ets98B recognized the same core sequence, but differed in their preferences for 3′ flanking sequences.
source: Likewise, the class IV ETS family protein SPDEF and its ortholog Ets98B recognized the same core sequence, but differed in their preferences for 3′ flanking sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of ETS protein binding specificities, supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: In some isolated cases, specificities of orthologous TFs can diverge over long evolutionary time.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that in some isolated cases, specificities of orthologous TFs can diverge over long evolutionary time.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the few cases of divergent specificities observed

claim: TFs and TF DBDs recognize the same, relatively long sites, with more than half of all models being >10 bp in length.
source: Consistent with our earlier data, we found that TFs and TF DBDs recognize the same, relatively long sites, with more than half of all models being >10 bp in length (Jolma et al., 2013).
